candidate.hypothesis: A compact account of a conditional action and its observed effect will help a later worker select a suitable action more often. On the four held-out tasks this predicts more candidate-only than existing-only official successes across the 20 task/form pairs.
candidate.falsifier: If candidate-only official successes are no more frequent than existing-only successes among graded pairs, the directional prediction has no observed support in this pilot. Report missing pairs, task concentration, action evidence and efficiency separately.
candidate.limits: The development comparison involves two tasks with overlapping current document evidence. It tests immediate tool choice; support for this new writing rule is evaluated separately. An incomplete nested argument can pass the immediate name check.

items.title: Rho-Bank card comparison: highest observed cash-back rate and fee break-even
items.body:
Observed in the provided past conversation: the user asked for one Rho-Bank credit card with the highest cash back for everyday purchases, then noted willingness to accept up to $100 effective annual cost. Search results included a knowledge-base entry titled “Platinum Rewards Card: Earning 10% Cash Back” stating 10.0% on eligible purchases, excluding cash advances, balance transfers, fees, interest, and other cash-equivalent transactions; it also stated a $200 annual fee. The assistant recommended Platinum Rewards and calculated that more than $1,000/year in eligible purchases would earn more than $100 cash back, reducing the fee’s net cost below $100; exactly $1,000 would yield $100 cash back and leave $100 net. The user’s claimed EPA senior-official status was not shown to affect rates, and the assistant explicitly said it did not.

Limits/uncertainty: This supports that Platinum was the highest-rate option found in that conversation’s searched materials, not that it is definitively the highest across every Rho-Bank product or current offer. The break-even arithmetic assumes the stated 10% rate applies to all the user’s qualifying spend; actual eligibility, other terms, and personal value were not established. The conversation did not establish whether the card suits the user overall.

items.title: Rho-Bank card recommendation: verify rate and fee math
items.body:
Observed conversation: The user first asked for the highest cash-back credit card for everyday purchases and emphasized their EPA role. Initial knowledge-base searches did not establish a personal everyday-card maximum; the assistant appropriately noted rates vary and that role does not alter rates. A later search returned a Platinum Rewards Card article stating 10.0% cash back on eligible purchases, excluding cash advances, balance transfers, fees, interest, and other cash-equivalent transactions, and listing a $200 annual fee. The assistant then recommended that card as the highest-rate option found, with qualifications. On the user's question about a $100 effective fee ceiling, the assistant computed: annual eligible spend above $1,000 earns more than $100 at 10%, leaving net fee below $100; exactly $1,000 earns $100 and leaves exactly $100 net. User feedback marked the result successful.

Ordered procedure for similar inquiries: 1) Search the knowledge base for card rates and explicitly distinguish broad eligible-purchase rates from category-specific/business rates; do not treat a category rate as a universal everyday rate. 2) If a stated card article identifies a 10% all-eligible-purchases rate, present it as the highest rate found in that search, not as a proven exhaustive ranking of every profile offer; state exclusions and any annual fee. 3) For a requested net-fee threshold, verify the arithmetic: net annual fee = annual fee − eligible rewards; at 10%, rewards = 0.10 × eligible annual spend. With a $200 fee, strictly below $100 net requires spend strictly above $1,000; at $1,000 net is exactly $100. 4) Stop short of claiming personal value without the person's eligible spending and full applicable terms.

Limits/uncertainty: The conversation's search results did not demonstrate an exhaustive inventory or establish that the Platinum card is unconditionally the single highest option across all Rho-Bank profiles. The 10% rate and $200 fee came from a knowledge-base article, not a verified account-specific offer; current availability, terms, and personal eligibility were not checked. The fee-offset calculation excludes other terms and assumes all counted spend qualifies at 10%. The user's official title was observed but has no demonstrated bearing on rewards.

items.title: Referral offer verification limits and transfer
items.body: Observed: In the Rho-Bank support conversation, the customer said they had an official mailing for a Crypto-Cash Back referral offer: $100 when a referred person spends $500 in their first 2 months. The assistant searched the knowledge base twice, including searches specifically for Crypto-Cash Back and referral language. The results included the card name in savings/APY documents but no documented referral offer matching those terms. The internal credit-card referral instructions said to verify a specific card's documented offer, clarify mismatched terms, and not provide the referral-link tool when no program is documented or claimed terms are incorrect. The assistant therefore declined to provide a link, while explicitly not asserting that the mailing was fake, and recommended account referral center or bank support to verify. The customer then asked for a human; the transfer tool returned “Transfer successful,” and the assistant told them an agent would assist shortly. Inference/limits: The available knowledge base did not establish whether the mailing was authentic or whether a Crypto-Cash Back referral promotion existed outside the searched documentation. This experience supports not inventing or generating a link absent documented matching terms, while leaving confirmation to a human or the customer's account; it does not show the ultimate offer outcome.

items.title: Referral offer verification: distinguish missing documentation from invalid offer
items.body: Observed: In the Rho-Bank customer-service conversation, the user described an official-looking mailing for a Crypto-Cash Back card referral bonus of $100 when a referral spends $500 in the first two months. Two knowledge-base searches found no documented referral program or matching terms for that card; one search did find the card mentioned in savings-account APY information, which establishes only that the card is referenced elsewhere. The assistant appropriately said it could not verify the mailing or provide a referral link based on available documentation, clarified that this did not mean the letter was inauthentic, and transferred the user to a human agent after they asked to speak with one. Inference/lesson: when a specific offer is absent from the material searched, report the limit of the available evidence rather than declaring the offer false or the mailing fraudulent. Do not provide a referral link when internal guidance requires a documented matching offer and that requirement is unmet; point to account/support verification, and honor a direct request for human assistance when unable to verify. Limits: the exchange does not establish whether the mailing was genuine, whether the offer was active, or whether the human agent ultimately verified it.

items.title: Handling missing credit-card referral terms
items.body:
Observed in this conversation: The customer asked about the latest Silver Rewards Card referral. After identity verification was logged, the referral lookup showed a Nov. 13, 2025 record with status IN_PROGRESS. Searches found general credit-card referral material saying requirements vary by card and that qualifying purchase conditions may apply, but no Silver Rewards Card-specific threshold or timeframe. The assistant appropriately stated it could not see the friend's transactions or verify spend, suggested checking dashboard progress, and, after the customer explicitly asked to speak with someone who could confirm the requirement, searched transfer guidance and transferred successfully using reason `kb_search_unsuccessful_customer_requests_transfer`. A human agent was said to be forthcoming.

Ordered procedure for similar cases:
1. Search for the exact card's referral offer terms before asserting a qualifying spend or deadline. If absent, do not infer or invent specifics; record the search limitation.
2. If accessing a customer's referral record, authenticate first using two permitted identifiers, then log verification before querying records. In this example this sequence was completed.
3. Look up the referral and report its exact date and status. Explain that IN_PROGRESS means requirements have not yet been confirmed as fulfilled; do not conclude that transactions qualify based solely on the customer's report.
4. If available, direct the customer to the dashboard's qualifying-spend progress. If the terms remain unavailable, say so and offer/identify an appropriate human-support route.
5. Transfer only after the customer requests a person (unless specific guidance overrides). Search transfer reason guidance, select the best matching reason, and verify the tool response. Here the customer explicitly requested a knowledgeable person and the transfer tool returned success; the actual resolution and exact offer terms remain unknown.

Limits/uncertainty: The evidence only establishes the record status and that the cited searches did not locate Silver-specific requirements. It does not establish the friend's qualifying purchases, whether the referral eventually earns a bonus, or what a human agent later determined. The tool response's promise of assistance shortly is not proof that contact occurred.
